items.abstract: <jats:p>We establish that the sequences formed by logarithms and by "fractional" powers of integers, as well as the sequence of prime numbers, are non-holonomic, thereby answering three open problems of Gerhold [El. J. Comb. 11 (2004), R87].  Our proofs depend on basic complex analysis, namely a conjunction of the Structure Theorem for singularities of solutions to linear differential equations and of an Abelian theorem.  A brief discussion is offered regarding the scope of singularity-based methods and several naturally occurring sequences are proved to be non-holonomic.</jats:p>
title: On the Non-Holonomic Character of Logarithms, Powers, and the $n$th Prime Function

items.abstract: This chapter studies exponential functions and logarithms. Mathematically, one of the simplest exponential equations is y = ax where a is a constant, x is the controlled variable, and y is the observed variable. The chapter then looks at exponential graphs, which follow general shapes called growth or decay. The crucial difference between these two types of graphs is the sign of the argument and the sign before the exponential. The chapter also considers logarithms as the inverse of exponential functions and in bases other than e. It explains the laws of logarithms, the relationship between ln and log, and numerical calculations with logarithms. Multiplication and division problems are simplified when using the first and second laws of logarithms, respectively. Meanwhile, the third law of logarithms allows for a simple, alternative approach to calculate roots.
title: Powers II
The Expression of the nth Power of a Number in Terms of the nth Powers of Other Numbers, n Being any Integer; and the Deduction of Some Interesting Properties of Prime Numbers

items.abstract: <jats:p>Finding formulae for the nth prime is one of the important topics in number theory. For many years, the enthusiasm for searching for prime number formulas has remained high. In this paper, I give two expressions of the nth prime.</jats:p>
title: Two expressions of the nth prime
On Prime Powers and Symbolic Prime Powers.

<jats:p>Abstract:
The Prime Spectrum Model investigates the connection between the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function and the distribution of prime numbers using spectral analysis. A wave function is constructed from 40,000 zeros and analyzed using Fourier Transform and Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT). Detected frequency peaks align with the natural logarithms of prime numbers, achieving RMSE = 0.0600 and Spearman correlation &#8776; 1.0. The model successfully identifies the first 50 primes and extrapolates to higher ones. This work offers insights into the Riemann Hypothesis and opens applications in physics, signal processing, and complexity theory.</jats:p>
title: Prime Spectrum Model Mapping Riemann Zeta Zeros to Prime Logarithms via Signal Processing

items.abstract: <jats:p>Consider both the Logarithmic integral, Li(x)=limϵ→0∫01−ϵdulnu+∫1+ϵxdulnu, and the prime counting function π(x)=∑p≤x1. From several recently developed known effective bounds on the prime counting function of the general form |π(x)−Li(x)|<ax(lnx)bexp−clnx for x≥x0 and known constants {a,b,c,x0}, we shall show that it is possible to establish exponentially tight effective upper and lower bounds on the prime number theorem. For x≥x∗, where x∗≤max{x0,17}, we have the following: Li(x)1+a(lnx)b+1exp−clnx<π(x)< Li(x)1−a(lnx)b+1exp−clnx. These bounds provide a modern, and very clean and explicit, version of the celebrated prime number theorem. Furthermore, it is possible to establish exponentially tight effective upper and lower bounds on the location of the nth prime. Specifically, we find that pn<Li−1n1+a(ln[nlnn])b+1exp−cln[nlnn] for n≥n∗, whereas pn>Li−1n1−a(ln[nlnn])b+1exp−cln[nlnn] for n≥n∗. Herein, the range of validity is explicitly bounded by some calculable constant n∗ satisfying n∗≤max{π(x0),π(17),π((1+e−1) exp2(b+1)c2)}. These bounds provide very clean and up-to-date and explicit information on the location of the nth prime number. Many other fully explicit bounds along these lines can easily be developed. Overall this article presents a general algorithmic approach to converting bounds on |π(x)−Li(x)| into somewhat clearer information regarding the primes.</jats:p>
title: The nth Prime Exponentially

items.abstract: This chapter introduces the exponential and logarithmic function. It is important to understand these new functions because they are an essential tool in any economic analysis involving variables that are growing through time. The logarithmic function can be applied to solving compound growth problems in which the unknown is the number of years over which a given amount of growth occurs. The logarithmic function is also used quite widely in economics in other contexts, for example, in a logarithmic specification for the demand function.
title: The exponential function and logarithms
